theses.summary: Four claims: (1) HBM/memory supply constrains AI until 2028; (2) the compute-scaling era is over, software-hardware co-design wins next; (3) general-purpose chips give way to custom silicon; (4) the opportunity has moved to 'logistics' -- advanced packaging, new storage, silicon photonics, edge/dedicated chips -- and to integrating AI into industries rather than building the largest models.

claims.statement: Memory/HBM supply constrains AI development through 2028
claims.assessment: Mechanism well supported -- the memory wall is a decades-old architectural fact and HBM capacity is genuinely tight. But the named date is a forecast, not a fact, and capacity expansions are announced.

claims.statement: Piling on compute is over; software-hardware co-design wins
claims.assessment: Dennard scaling ended ~2006 and Moore's law is slowing, so the premise is sound. 'Over' is overstated -- GPUs remain dominant and custom silicon coexists rather than replaces.

claims.statement: Advanced packaging and silicon photonics are the golden tracks
claims.assessment: CoWoS packaging being a real bottleneck is well documented. Photonics is earlier and more speculative.

claims.statement: Custom and edge silicon displaces general-purpose chips
claims.assessment: Custom silicon at Apple/Google/Amazon/Meta is real and growing. 'Displaces' is the overstatement; these coexist.

claims.statement: Biggest 5y growth is integrating AI into industries, not larger models
claims.assessment: Plausible and widely held, but as stated it has no observable consequence that could refute it. Recorded, not testable.
